newsitem.title: USA: Clinton repeats call for educational standards.
newsitem.headline: Clinton repeats call for educational standards.

text.p: President Clinton took his educational crusade on the road Monday, using the Maryland State House as a bully pulpit to argue for national educational standards.

"The most important thing we can do in education is to hold our students to high standards," Clinton told Maryland state legislators, criticising local school boards who oppose national standards on the grounds that they consitute federal interference.
Speaking in the nation's oldest state legislature continually in service, Clinton promoted his plan to develop national reading tests for fourth graders and national math tests for eighth graders.

"(To) anybody who says that a country as big and diverse as ours can't possibly have national standards...I say from Maryland to Michigan to Montana, reading is reading and math is math," he said. "No school board is in charge of algebra and no state legislature can enact the laws of physics."
Clinton, who emphasised education in his State of the Union speech last Tuesday, also said the Business Roundtable, an industry and trade group, had endorsed his standards effort.
On the issue of welfare, Clinton exhorted businessmen and states to help implement last year's welfare reform law and urged them to help find jobs for welfare recipients.
The law ended the 61-year federal entitlement to welfare, limiting benefits to five years and requiring most recipients to work after two years.
